name: Bromus
common_group: Bromes — compare 4 installed species and native vs introduced risks
look_here_first: BROMUS: every species has separate MULTI-FLOWERED SPIKELETS along a branched PANICLE, not a tight Hordeum/Elymus true spike. For the four installed species: JAPANESE = introduced annual, flexuous long-awned head with more GLUME VEINS (often 3–5 lower/7 upper); TEXAS BROME = native Texas annual with ONE-veined lower/THREE-veined upper glume; LANCEOLATE = introduced annual with VERY LARGE ~25–50 mm 8–20-flowered narrow spikelets; WOODLAND BROME = native perennial with truly HAIRY lemmas, moist woods. RESCUEGRASS is COMPARISON ONLY: broad flat oatlike short/no-awn spikelets.

comparison_lesson.title: Four canonical bromes plus rescuegrass — anatomy-first field key
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: Japonicus introduced + higher glume veins vs rare native texensis 1/3; lanceolatus giant narrow 8–20-flowered; pubescens perennial hairy lemma; catharticus broad flat short/no-awn comparison.
quick_split: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair.
Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle.

Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma.

Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm.

Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
guardrails: All four Bromus cards already installed. B. catharticus RESCUEGRASS is comparison ONLY, not an added approved species.
Kew and FNA disagree on precise B. japonicus spikelet size ranges; do not promote narrow cutoff as decisive.
Texas brome lemma apex entire in FNA versus 2-toothed in other accounts; use glume veins and matched lemma/awn instead.
Bromus pubescens old photo only 389×589, so actual lemma hair macro remains a gap.
No native-by-county audit in this finishing pass; native at broad scale does not establish Hays county occurrence.
field_photo_steps: Count distinct FLORETS (many overlapping LEMMAS) within ONE spikelet.
Photograph WHOLE PANICLE: drooping flexuous, large stiff-lanceolate, broad flat or wooded perennial architecture.
Check ROOTED duration: pubescens perennial; Japanese, lanceolate and texensis annual; rescuegrass short-lived annual OR perennial depending treatment.
For native Texas vs introduced Japanese, backlight LOWER/UPPER GLUMES: native often 1 and 3 longitudinal nerves, introduced Japanese often 3–5 and 7, with variation.
Photograph LEMMA and AWN side-by-side with ruler. Don't conflate awn tip, length of floret body or glume.
Compare 1-mm botanical photos against original source-tagged pictures; if anatomy absent keep Bromus sp.

key_characters: Annual cool-season bunch grass; senesces after seed set.
Panicle often open or nodding with thin flexuous branches, sometimes conspicuously kinked.
Spikelets typically contain 6–12 florets; published size descriptions differ (Oklahoma State 15–25 mm; FNA 20–40 mm), so length is not a stand-alone ID character.
Lemma awns frequently longer than on woodland brome, sometimes ~15 mm; lengths overlap other annual bromes.
Soft retrorse hairs on lower sheaths and often bent lower culms.
comparisons.against_group: Compared to B. lanceolatus, usually shorter spikelets with fewer florets and more relaxed/kinked drooping branches; lanceolatus often has ~25–50 mm spikelets with 8–20 florets. Compared to native B. texensis, note Texas brome generally shorter 6–10 mm awns and requires lemma/branch dissection, not habitat alone. Unlike perennial B. pubescens, this is an annual and usually shorter-lived.

key_characters: Annual grass with often ascending or spreading branches, less filmy and flexuous than Japanese brome.
Lanceolate to oblong elongated spikelets often ~25–50 mm with 8–20 florets, much larger than typical Japanese brome.
Mature fertile lemma usually ~12–18 mm and awned around 6–12 mm in GrassBase treatment; measurements overlap.
Membranous ligule, hairy to nearly smooth sheaths, variable leaf-blade pubescence.
Awn arises from notched lemma tip; detailed shape/length and glume nerves require hand lens.
comparisons.against_group: Introduced B. japonicus has slender, sometimes kinked/nodding panicle branches; its variable 15–40 mm reported spikelet lengths overlap other bromes. Native B. texensis has 1-veined lower and 3-veined upper glumes, 9–15 mm lemmas and straight 4–8 mm awns (FNA). Compare mature dissected spikelets. B. pubescens is a perennial of woodland understory with hairy lemmas and a loose drooping head; do not decide from habitat alone.

key_characters: Perennial in shady moist woods rather than short-lived cool-season weed.
Erect to arching leafy culms often 0.6–1.5 m high, with relatively broad 6–19 mm grass blades.
Open spreading/drooping panicle generally ~10–25 cm long.
Multi-flowered spikelets ~13–30 mm, often with 5–10 florets.
Lemma short straight awn usually ~3–8 mm; surfaces often fine-hairy, but this cannot be confirmed from current photo.
Closed sheaths with soft retrorse hairs, ligule short membranous; botanical treatments differ slightly in typical lengths.
comparisons.against_group: Unlike the three other currently installed Bromus cards, B. pubescens is PERENNIAL and often found in shaded moist woodland understory. Japanese brome is a small-spikeleted annual with flexuous panicle branches; B. lanceolatus has unusually long, many-flowered annual spikelets; B. texensis is an annual with shorter awns and requires mature glume/lemma comparison. Habitat or hairiness alone cannot clinch this one.

key_characters: Annual (not perennial) native Texas brome of open woodland/grassland sites.
Sheaths with soft recurved/retrorse hairs; blades often ~3–7 mm wide.
Fertile lemmas typically ~9–12 mm, with a two-toothed apex and one 6–10 mm awn.
Spikelets multi-flowered, borne on branching panicle.
Fertilizing yellow anthers may be conspicuous at flowering, but are common to other grass taxa.
comparisons.against_group: B. japonicus is an introduced annual with slender, flexuous and sometimes nodding panicle branches; reported spikelet size overlaps native B. texensis, so use lower/upper glume nerves (typically 3–5/7 versus 1/3). B. lanceolatus has densely many-flowered longer lanceolate spikelets; B. pubescens is a woodland perennial with hairy lemmas. Green slender spikelets alone are never enough for a native-versus-introduced call.

comparison_matrix.title: Bromus practical 5-species evidence matrix
rows: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair.

Open macro: overlapping lemmas have long often twisted/recurving awns from below their apices; source descriptions vary considerably in spikelet length. Do not use a 10–15 mm cutoff to exclude Japanese brome.
Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle.
Compare long often pointed spikelets with Japanese brome's often smaller fewer florets, but both dimensions vary; check true lemma body and awn attachment at 10–20×.

Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma.
A mature persistent perennial tuft/crown and hairy lemmas support pubescens, unlike short-lived Japanese, lanceolate and Texas annuals.

Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm.

This 1/3 vein pair distinguishes from Japanese's commonly higher 3–5/7 vein counts. The lemma apex described as entire by FNA but sometimes toothed in other treatments: DO NOT force an ID from 'two teeth'.

Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
Large flattened overlapping V/oat-like florets contrast with Japanese brome's narrow long-awned units and lanceolate brome's narrower long densely floret spikelets.

what_to_teach_crew: Brome spikelets have several actual FLORETS, unlike single-seed grass ID assumptions.
Do not remove a possible native Texas brome because Japanese brome has similar nodding awned branches; photograph glume veins first.
Rescuegrass B. catharticus is already common in disturbed Texas habitats but is comparison-only in our learner, not installed.
Woodland perennial pubescens can have hairy foliage like annual invasives: check rooted crown and lemma surface (different organs).
The fast wide-head rescuegrass contrast is broad and FLAT with short/no awns, not only a 'droops' decision.
True source photographs have individual author and licenses; no arrows to unreadable glume veins.

items.label: RESCUEGRASS (comparison only) — broad flattened drooping spikelets
items.image_role: True living Bromus catharticus plant with hanging relatively wide flat green spikelets and leafy basal tuft at creek bank
items.caption: Australian-source mature rescuegrass shows broad, flattened spikelets in a more open hanging head; they overlap like small flat oat grains. Its lemmas bear short or no awns compared with Japanese brome's longer and more divergent awns. A basal tuft is visible; no microscopic glumes/ligule or annual-versus-perennial proof is available from this photograph.
items.why_it_matters: Rescuegrass is introduced in Texas and often appears in disturbed lawns, riparian margins and cool-season seed mixes. Broad flat short/awnless florets are a practical alternative to the much narrower long-awned annual bromes.
items.creator: Harry Rose / Macleay Grass Man
items.photo_status: Original Wikimedia Commons 960×~700 landscape crop source inspected 2026-10-21; CC BY 2.0 attribution and Australian setting confirmed. Arrows to gross visible drooping spikelets and base; no microscopic lemma claims.
